comments.author: @TheMemeRepository
comments.text:
Definitely sounds like a knock-on effect from the power of suggestion.

Her friends & family told her that this AI voice sounds like her, she listened to it with that in mind, and because we artists aren't the best at emotional regulation, her brain ran away with that narrative, ironically, harming another actress in the process (potentially, depending on the contract).

To me, I didn't even think they sounded remotely similar until someone pointed it out, and even then, the best I can give it is they share a similar vibe. They're within the same type, maybe? But Sky isn't the only voice available is the thing, and they're only going to add more voices over time. You need a lot of different voices to cover the vast range of tones that people may desire from a personal assistant, so it's only natural that a voice in Scarlett's range was going to be sampled at some point.

But like I said, the power of suggestion is strong, especially when it pairs with a pre-existing bias. There's a lot of resistance against AI right now, so when people see the headline "ChatGPT stole celebrity's voice" people are naturally going to pounce on that without probing, and when others present them with the facts as we know them, they will sink deeper into emotional reasoning to justify their initial presumption, which can be seen with statements like "It's so obvious, they even asked her again right before announcement" as if that's some smoking gun, rather than a vague event we don't have all the details for.

But yeah, I don't really blame people for acting irrationally while everything is emotionally charged, and I think it's important to discuss why people tend to act this way, but it's also frustrating when, from my perspective, this is such a nothing burger in the scheme of all the Open AI drama.

comments.text:
Here's the thing: you don't own your "voice" or your "look". You own your actual voice recordings and your actual pictures, insofar as if someone uses ACTUAL images of YOU on their product/production without your permission, you can sue them (and you don't even really own those if they're taken in public and not used for promotional purposes - the person making the photo/recording owns them); however, if a voice actor happens to have a similar voice (even if they play up that similarity to your voice) or a different person happens to look a lot like you, it's still legal for them to perform and use their voice/face commercially.

It would be psychotic if every thin, pretty, young girl in a video had to pay licensing fees to (or get permission from) whichever popular actress or singer they looked/sang most like. There are even professional look-alikes who make good money from their resemblance to a famous person, and it's 100% legal as long as they're not claiming TO BE that person. In no sane universe would we ever say to people, "I'm sorry, you can't use your voice/face commercially because ScarJo beat you to it. She owns that tone/timbre/cheek bone structure/whatever."

You don't even own your "style" - someone can paint just like you do as long as they're not trying to pass their paintings off as being painted by you. You can even copy a famous painting and sell it as long as you're honest about its origins.

AI has thrown a bit of a wrench in this with the whole "voice cloning" tech (e.g. the fake Drake songs) and those probably cross the line. Also, I think it's clearly reasonable for artists to object when an AI has been trained to produce a near-perfect simulation of their voices or images - not just something vaguely or stylistically similar. But here's where it gets murky: what if a sound-alike voice actor was used to train an AI with a Drake-ish voice. It wasn't trained on Drake, it only sounds 90% like Drake, and the other person (who had every right to use their voice and has been compensated) signed off on using their voice. While there would almost certainly be a lawsuit, I can't imagine it would ultimately win.
